To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
time perception and memory encoding are compromised in emotional situations and are associated with activity in the amygdala and insula.
time perception and memory are functionally linked in emotionally aversive contexts.

1) time perception is compromised in emotionally aversive situations, 2) memory for emotionally aversive events is enhanced in these situations, 3) the two phenomena are functionally linked and 4) the neural networks underlying the association between time perception and memory are in the superior frontal gyr, amygdala, insula and putaman.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of the interplay between time perception and memory encoding in emotional contexts.
the question of how the brain integrates the experience of time and emotion, and how this integration is linked with memory.
the interplay between memory and time perception in emotional situations and provides new insights into the neural basis of this association.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

time perception and memory are functionally linked, but that the link is not necessarily direct, but rather is indirect, and that the neural networks underlying this link are complex and not yet completely understood. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
the insula and the putamen are part of the neural network that is involved in time perception and memory processing in emotional situations.
the brain is able to process emotionally aversive stimuli in a more detailed manner than neutral stimuli and that this processing is associated with a time perception bias.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain processes emotional events faster and more efficiently, but this processing is at the cost of time perception accuracy, which is distorted in emotional situations.
the brain's ability to process information in emotional situations is enhanced, at least in the case of aversive situations, but at the expense that the time perception is distorted.
the brain processes aversive events faster and more efficiently, and this is reflected in time perception errors and better memory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
time perception and memory are not independent of one another and are in fact closely linked in emotionally aversive situations.
the brain's ability to process emotional information is so powerful that it can distort the perception of time itself.
the brain's ability to perceive time accurately is compromised when we are emotionally aroused, and the neural networks that mediate time perception and emotional processing are functionally linked.
